summary: Source-anchored research for solana-py solders and @solana/web3.js and @solana/kit. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: @solana/kit is the renamed 2.x line of @solana/web3.js. It is functional (no classes except SolanaError), fully tree-shakable, uses Web Crypto Ed25519 so key and signing operations are async, supports native bigint, and has zero third-party dependencies. It is not backward-compatible with web3.js 1.x. (high confidence)

Kit has no Connection or Transaction classes. Moving a web3.js v1 codebase to Kit means rewriting every call site, and libraries such as Anchor's TypeScript client did not plug into Kit. The @solana/compat package offers conversion helpers between legacy and Kit types. (high confidence)

Guidance after the compromise: upgrade to 1.95.8 (even when pinned to latest) or downgrade to a version before 1.95.6, and rotate any suspect authority keys, including multisigs, program authorities and server keypairs. Cyfrin added: check yarn.lock or package-lock.json for the bad versions, and keep strict version control and lockfiles. (high confidence)

Anza's root-cause analysis says the phished publisher entered a username and password and completed two-factor authentication on an attacker-run clone of the npm site, so two-factor authentication did not stop the attack. (medium confidence)

In Python, solders (Rust-backed bindings by Kevin Heavey) supplies the core types: Keypair, Pubkey, Instruction, MessageV0, VersionedTransaction, signing and serialization, RPC request and response types, and an in-process LiteSVM. solders does not fetch blockhashes or send transactions; solana-py's AsyncClient does (get_latest_blockhash, send_transaction). solana-py builds on solders types, and its README says anything missing from it 'is probably in solders now'. Solana's docs name both packages and recommend solana-py for networking and async APIs. The solders tutorial recommends versioned transactions 'if you have a choice'. The two install separately (pip install solders; pip install solana). (high confidence)

Upgrading to web3.js v3 silently changes Connection's default commitment from finalized to confirmed. The code compiles unchanged, so the compiler cannot flag it; the official migration guide says 'omitted commitment now defaults to confirmed rather than finalized'. A bot that relied on finalized reads must pass the commitment explicitly on the Connection or per call, and should test against a real node because mocked tests keep passing with the old default. (high confidence)

In Python, solders (Rust bindings) supplies the core types (Keypair, Pubkey, Instruction, MessageV0, VersionedTransaction), RPC request and response types, and a LiteSVM test VM (solders.litesvm) that Solana's docs call a much faster alternative to solana-test-validator. solders does no networking. solana-py is built on solders and supplies AsyncClient, SolanaWsClient and SPL Token helpers. Solana's docs list both under community clients and recommend solana-py for networking and async RPC. (high confidence)
